title: The Great Slogan Vanishing Act
caption:
Your favorite brand's slogan didn't disappear. It chose minimalism instead.

Taglines are being stripped away at record pace.
But here's what the data won't tell you: this move works best when a brand already occupies space in your mind.

Apple didn't drop "Think Different" because it was outdated.
They did it because everyone already knew what they stood for.

Removal becomes a statement when recognition is assumed.
For emerging brands, silence can read as uncertainty.

The real question isn't whether you should have a slogan.
It's whether yours still serves a purpose.

What's your brand's reason for existing in the conversation today?

slides.headline: Nike keeps 'Just Do It'—and thrives
slides.body: While others strip down, Nike invests in slogan reinforcement through athlete partnerships and cultural moments. Strategy matters more than trend-following.

slides.headline: 97% of consumers say brand familiarity drives purchase decisions
slides.body: Removing taglines works only when the brand itself is already iconic. Familiarity trumps clever copy every time.

slides.headline: Don't follow the trend. Understand it.
slides.body: Audit your brand's actual recognition level. If it's not instantly familiar, your slogan might be your strongest asset—not your burden.

title: Medellín's Escalator Experiment
caption:
These outdoor escalators moved 28,000 people daily up a hillside once deemed too dangerous to enter.

Medellín installed three outdoor escalators in 2004, connecting the hillside comunas to the city below. The system cut travel time from 45 minutes to 5 minutes, transforming mobility for residents of steep, informally built neighborhoods.

The escalators became a global symbol of urban reinvention, featured in museums and urban planning conferences. But in 2020, the city removed one section, citing maintenance costs and security concerns.

Infrastructure reshaped movement, but couldn't resolve deep inequality. Violence decreased, but economic opportunities remained concentrated in the city center.

The escalator experiment showed what's possible — and what's not.

What does truly equitable urban infrastructure look like?

slides.headline: Medellín's Outdoor Escalators: Rise and Partial Fall
slides.body: In Comuna 13, twelve elevated escalators helped connect one of Colombia's most marginalized neighborhoods to downtown — at peak usage carrying 28,000 riders per day.

slides.headline: 28,000 People Rode Daily Before 2023
slides.body: City data from 2022 shows that nearly 28,000 people used the outdoor escalator system in Comuna 13 each day.
slides.footnote: Alcalde de Medellín, Informe de Movilidad 2022

slides.headline: Comuna 13 Was Among Latin America's Most Dangerous Areas
slides.body: In the early 2000s, homicide rates in Comuna 13 exceeded 90 per 100,000 residents annually. Violence and isolation defined life for many here.
slides.footnote: Observatorio de Seguridad Ciudadana de Medellín, 2005

slides.headline: Escalators Were Part of a Bolder Plan
slides.body: They weren't standalone fixes. The city paired them with cable cars, libraries, parks, and schools as part of its 'social urbanism' strategy.
slides.footnote: UN-Habitat, 'Urban Transformation and Safety in Comuna 13', 2012

slides.headline: $2 Million Built Twelve Escalators
slides.body: That's modest compared to metro rail systems. Funding came largely from national infrastructure grants during a period of major civic upgrades.
slides.footnote: Banco de la República, memorias fiscales 2007–2009

slides.headline: Escalators Became a Tourist Attraction
slides.body: Guided tours now climb them as monuments of redemption. What began as commuter infrastructure became symbolic capital.

slides.headline: Three Escalators Removed in 2023
slides.body: Maintenance costs and low ridership led to partial dismantling. Only nine remain operational today.
slides.footnote: El Colombiano, 'Retiran escaleras mecánicas en Comuna 13', 2023

slides.headline: Did They Actually Move Lives Forward?
slides.body: Critics say accessibility gains didn't translate to jobs or mobility outcomes for youth. And some residents felt paternalized by the global spotlight.
slides.footnote: Academia Nacional de Ciencias Sociales, 2018; El Espectador

slides.headline: Can Infrastructure Lift Inequality—or Just Perform It?
slides.body: Medellín's escalators sparked hope and headlines—but lasting change needs more than moving steps. Share if you think cities can build both equity and identity.

title: Why Your Routine Dies on Day 4, Not Day 1
caption: Day 4 is a neurochemical wall, not a discipline problem. A 2022 Founders Forum survey of 487 early-stage founders found 23% abandoned their morning routines specifically on day 4 when operational stress spiked. A PNAS study found ventral striatum dopamine response dropped 22% after four consecutive days of cognitive demand. This looks like lack of discipline but is actually a neurochemical wall that hits after one full stress cycle completes. The fix is not to push harder. The fix is to remove one decision before day 4 hits. Save this for your next routine. Send it to a founder who quits too early.

title: Why Long Brand Names Fade After Ten
caption:
Long brand names lose you after midnight.

The brain truncates unfamiliar words at three syllables once decision fatigue sets in. This is not obvious because we assume recognition survives any hour.

It doesn’t.

Save this if it gave you pause, or send it to someone who still believes longer is better.
